title: The Quiet Reef
author: OpaliteGames
selftext:
I grew up a two minute walk from the beach in California, but for the last decade and a half I've lived nowhere near an ocean and I miss it constantly. I wanted to build the underwater world that I visited daily for most of my life.

It's called The Quiet Reef. You're a diver in a big marine sanctuary. No combat and no timer (but there are missions if you want to complete them), nothing trying to kill you (besides one great white, but he mostly just wants to scare you). You explore, photograph stuff, fill out a field guide, guide schools of fish home, play with dolphins, feed turtles and slowly find letters from the person who built the sanctuary.

Some stuff that's in there right now:  
\- around 100 marine species.  
\-an old wreck you can swim through.  
\-caves that are pitch black except for the creatures that naturally glow  
\-day/night, weather, moon phases, aurora and meteor showers at night  
\-a camera mode and a photo board with shots to go find  
\-facts about every species you encounter

It runs in the browser with no download and it works on desktop and mobile (PC/Mac for the best experience with controller or mouse/keyboard)

I've been a game designer at several large studios for the past 15 years. There's always been a pile of projects I wanted to make but couldn't on my own because of time and resources. AI has finally helped make that possible. This isn’t a one-shot, it’s taken me months of fine tuning and no, it isn’t 100% AI made. It’s not out yet (soon), but figured I’d give you guys a sneak peek! In the end, I built the game for me, but figured others might enjoy it too.

comments.author: Reign2294
comments.body: Would you consider sharing how you animated the schools, whale, and manta and such? I am developing a 2d game, but having those elements in the parallax screen would be great i think.

replies.author: HBSurfPhoto
replies.body:
Happy to explain!. When I originally started working on the game I was hand animating everything, but quickly realized that task was too large for making everything move the way I wanted. It's one area that AI has helped out substantially. I explain the creature's movement and it does the following:

Every creature has it's own species logic and is moved around by a path with randomization in specified areas. They each have a wave running through their body from head to tail. Give each animal its own timing so they never move in sync. In 2D you can do the wave by bending a strip of points.

* Schools - each fish avoids its neighbor, swims the way they're swimming in a set height and width &stays near the group. The whole school slowly drifts in a wandering direction. 
* Big fish tornado - too many fish for rules, so each one just circles a central point at its own height. Fish at the outside are drawn brighter and the back ones dimmer. Very cheap, great for far layers.
* Whale - rare and slow. It beats its tail roughly once every five seconds and alternates strokes with long glides.
* Mantas - the flap is a wave rolling out to the wingtips, not a hinge. In the migration, each manta is a slightly different size and flaps on its own timing, but they all follow the same path with randomization up/down left/right to create variety.

Can definitely share more details if it helps!

replies.author: Reign2294
replies.body:
Oh this is great. Thank you. I will take as much detail as you're willing to offer haha. 

My main gameplay is in the foreground, but having a passing whale like you've animated would really breathe life into the scene. What tools did you use to make them? Blender? You said you were doing things by hand before. Does it help you to build a skeleton that can be animated? Or something else? 

I am more of a PS person myself, so forgive my lack of understanding in animation

replies.author: OpaliteGames
replies.body:
Nothing is a 3D model in the game anymore. The whale is built entirely in code now. A script builds the body from a table of measurements I took off a public NOAA side-view drawing of a humpback, giving the height of its back and belly at 17 points from nose to tail.

Some of the other animals (the shark, dolphins, turtle and jellyfish) do go through Blender. A Python script runs inside it to build and export them as code. Each point on the model just stores a few numbers saying how far along the body it is and how much it should bend. The game reads those numbers and moves the points every frame.

The movement itself is the wave I described before. It travels from head to tail, it's barely there at the front and strong at the tail, and its strength and speed change over time. The flippers are the one exception: they rotate around a pivot point at the shoulder, each on its own slow cycle.

For a whale in a 2D background a wave does the job better and is easier than using a skeleton. If you're already using a skeleton tool (Spine, DragonBones, Godot's Skeleton2D), that works too. Make a chain of bones down the body and set each bone's rotation from the same wave every frame, instead of keyframing it. Use the slope of the wave at that bone's position. You get the same result, just with bones in place of rope points.
